title: Canada in the New Monetary Order
author: Michael Hudson
desc: Análisis del sistema monetario internacional post-Bretton Woods.
tesis: Análisis del sistema monetario internacional después de que Nixon rompió el patrón oro en 1971. Hudson examina cómo Canadá, como economía dependiente de Estados Unidos, navega el nuevo orden donde el dólar flota libremente y EE.UU. exporta inflación al mundo.
ideas: La ruptura del patrón oro en 1971 transformó el sistema monetario internacional a favor de Estados Unidos.
Las economías dependientes como Canadá absorben las consecuencias de la política monetaria estadounidense.
El nuevo orden monetario permitió a EE.UU. financiar su imperio con déficits que el resto del mundo subsidia.
contexto: Publicado en 1978, siete años después de que Nixon rompiera el patrón oro. Hudson había trabajado como economista de balanza de pagos en Chase Manhattan Bank y asesorado al gobierno canadiense sobre flujos de capital. El libro analiza cómo Canadá, economía satélite de EE.UU., absorbió las consecuencias del nuevo orden monetario.

conexiones.razon: Super-Imperialism analiza el mismo sistema monetario pero desde la perspectiva del imperio.
Trade analiza las relaciones comerciales desiguales que el nuevo orden monetario profundiza.

deck.label: NotebookLM briefing — Canada's New Monetary Order

tl: Steuart calls gold 'the money of the world'

Classical models of international trade and finance were formulated in an epoch when domestic money and credit were based on gold, the metal that James Steuart called "the money of the world" in 1767. Countries that were not themselves gold producers could earn this gold either by exporting more than they imported, by selling their resources to foreign investors, or by borrowing. International trade and investment thus formed the ultimate foundation for the domestic bank credit needed to finance economic growth, at a time when this credit itself rested on gold reserves held by the banking system.
US 'Economy of High Wages' doctrine consolidates industrial lead

In general, growth in labour productivity has been associated with rising living standards. [...] In the nineteenth century the United States pursued an Economy of High Wages doctrine based on rising wage levels leading to an even more rapid growth in labour productivity. This reduced unit labour costs, thereby consolidating the United States' international industrial advantage. If greater austerity works to slow the growth in Canadian productivity, the country will become even more dependent on foreign suppliers.
England's Bank Reform Bill regulates only note issue

For many years the domestic money and credit system was only crudely understood by monetary officials and legislators. For instance, England's landmark 1844 Bank Reform Bill regulated only the banking system's ability to issue bank notes, leaving its credit-creating powers to its own discretion. This view reflected the theory of Ricardo and his followers, who imagined credit to be a transfer rather than a new creation of spending power so that bank loans merely shifted spending from one part of the economy to another.
United States turns to protective tariff after 1861

All of today's industrial nations have developed by means of protective tariffs whose revenues were used to fund a far-reaching system of internal improvements. Britain, in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, was emulated by continental Europe (led by France and Germany), the United States after 1861, Japan after the Meiji Restoration, and finally the socialist economies. For a while, these countries had to pay higher prices for domestic manufactured goods than they would have had they purchased these goods abroad. However, the excess spending was not simply dissipated, it was used to help put in place an industrial infrastructure.
Meiji Restoration: Japan builds industry behind tariffs

All of today's industrial nations have developed by means of protective tariffs whose revenues were used to fund a far-reaching system of internal improvements. Britain, in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, was emulated by continental Europe (led by France and Germany), the United States after 1861, Japan after the Meiji Restoration, and finally the socialist economies. [...] Countries that did not emulate the industrial nations, and which pursued their short-term advantage to the detriment of their long-term development, have fallen into the unenviable position of being hewers of wood and drawers of water.
Foreign capital finances Canadian Pacific Railroad and industry

For many centuries the development of Canada has been financed by foreign capital. The Canadian Pacific Railroad, much of Canadian industry, insurance companies, and other undertakings have been funded from abroad — either by direct investors who have retained ownership and control of these undertakings, or by lenders. [...] much of Canada's borrowing over the centuries has been to finance the cost of imports and productive capital required by the foreign-financed projects. The major type of foreign borrowing questioned in this monograph has been that portion of borrowing made simply for conversion into domestic currency for spending at home.
Canada's export prices collapse after WWI, foreign debt burden rises

Canada had good reason to borrow during this epoch — its borrowing represented buying time. The country's enormous but still largely untapped resource potential enabled it to repay its borrowers with interest. Basically Canada financed its international debts by exporting a rising flow of raw materials. However, when agricultural and mineral prices collapsed after World War I, and again in the Great Depression, the country found itself obliged to repay its foreign lenders and investors with fixed charges that represented a much greater purchasing power over Canadian exports than had been in effect at the time of original investment.
Keynes vs. Rueff on German reparations transfer problem

The argument over German reparations in the 1920s, between the structuralists (led by John Maynard Keynes in England and Harold Moulton in the United States) and the monetarists (led by Jacques Rueff of France and Bertil Ohlin of Sweden) concerned whether price changes and currency shifts would "naturally" balance international payments, or whether the problem was one of underlying productivity and trade patterns. The politically interested monetarist arguments did not fit the facts of the 1920s, and are even more obsolete today.
Britain restores pound to prewar parity, brings on depression

Prices were rolled back after each war — usually at the cost of depression and economic crisis as countries returned not only to gold itself but to gold at the prewar price level. (A more logical and less compulsive alternative would have been to accept the new postwar price level as a fact of life and to reinstate the gold standard on the basis of existing postwar relationships. This would have helped avoid the postwar depression that Britain brought upon itself in 1926 when it "heroically" restored the pound sterling to its prewar parity.)
Canadian tax code encourages foreign equity takeover

In fact, during the 1930s, the Canadian government adjusted the tax laws to encourage foreign equity investment in Canada rather than "indirect" investment in the form of loans and bond purchases. Dividend payments to foreign and domestic investors could be cut back easily in a period of economic depression and falling corporate earnings, whereas a reduction of interest paid on bonds and loans would put corporations in default and bankruptcy. Canada's incentives for foreign equity investment contributed to the subsequent foreign direct-investment takeover of its economy.
Great Depression collapses Canadian export prices again

Loans were repaid out of a rising flow of export proceeds... until the Great Depression collapsed world trade prices. [...] However, when agricultural and mineral prices collapsed after World War I, and again in the Great Depression, the country found itself obliged to repay its foreign lenders and investors with fixed charges that represented a much greater purchasing power over Canadian exports than had been in effect at the time of original investment. This increased the export burden of carrying the country's foreign debt.
Viner: capital-exporter epoch reverses with terms-of-trade cost

When borrowings cease but interest payments must continue, and especially when the time arrives for repayment of principal, Canada will have to face a reversal of all the price trends present during the period of capital borrowings. Canadian prices and wages will move down instead of up relatively to other countries. It will be necessary for Canada to sell her products at lower prices in order to induce her creditors to accept increased quantities thereof in payment of their claims to interest and principal. Canada will thus be able to liquidate her indebtedness and to obtain her necessary imports only on less advantageous terms.
Postwar world enters new epoch with little debt

The world economy entered the postwar epoch in 1946 with relatively little debt. Since then a rising share of income has been absorbed by debt service. Internationally, debt service is "crowding out" the ability of many countries to import goods, just as domestic debt service is crowding out new borrowing, investment, and consumer spending. Canada is by no means exempt from these trends.
US absorbs three-fourths of world monetary gold

After World War II the U.S. dollar took its place alongside gold as a prime vehicle in which central banks held their international reserves. Dollars remained scarce, being supplied to the world economy only as the United States ran a balance-of-payments deficit. Through 1950 the U.S. payments position remained in surplus, aggravating the world dollar shortage as the U.S. Treasury absorbed three-fourths of the world's monetary gold holdings. Dollars were freely convertible into gold by foreign central banks at a fixed price of $35 per troy ounce.
Soviet Union pioneers Eurodollar deposits after Korean War

Eurodollars represent dollar-denominated deposits held outside the United States. The credit superstructure based on these dollar deposits was originally the long string of U.S. dollar outflows following the Korean War. The Soviet Union was the first country to hold its dollars outside of the United States, wishing to avoid the possibility of U.S. seizure of these deposits in the event of sharper hostilities between the two countries. A decade later, in the 1960s, U.S. commercial banks began to transact foreign business in U.S. dollars as they sought to provide U.S. multinationals with a comprehensive package of banking services that included handling the finances of the overseas branches of these firms.
US overseas military spending pushes payments into deficit

Through the 1950s the United States' payments deficits were kept to modest proportions. But after 1960, overseas military spending pushed the U.S. payments position increasingly into deficit. As early as 1964, U.S. debts to foreign central banks soared beyond the value of gold held by the U.S. Treasury. Matters reached crisis proportions in early 1968. The Tet offensive in Vietnam triggered a massive increase in gold speculation by purchasers who believed that continued U.S. military spending abroad would drain U.S. gold to the point at which the U.S. Treasury and foreign central banks could no longer hold down its price to $35 an ounce.
Canada devalues into an expanding world economy

Today's world environment is quite different from that which existed when Canada last devalued its dollar in 1962. At that time world trade was expanding rapidly. Today the world economy is stagnating, and countries are resorting increasingly to protectionist policies in the face of continued recession. Thus, an export drive by Canada may encounter resistance abroad by an increasingly protectionist United States, as well as by Europe and Third World countries. (The United States takes two-thirds of Canada's exports, while the European Community and Third World countries each take one-eighth.) Even if world markets remain open, cost advantages resulting from depreciation may not be sufficient to ensure broader export markets.
Auto Pact signed between Canada and the United States

Canada had an active auto-parts industry operating near capacity in the mid-1960s when the Auto Pact was signed with the United States. The country's lower wage levels, its inexpensive dollar and the absence of U.S. tariffs led a number of companies to modernize their plants, and they enjoyed a thriving business. U.S. auto-parts manufacturers also modernized their plants, while the Canadian dollar rose in value to surpass the U.S. dollar and Canadian labour costs approached those of the United States. Under these conditions the decisive competitive factor became plant modernization — a generally neglected element in academic trade theory.
US imposes controls on overseas bank lending

After U.S. controls on overseas bank lending and direct investment were imposed in February 1965 — in conjunction with tighter domestic credit as the economy seriously overheated — the large international banks found themselves able to borrow through their foreign branches, whose original function had been to lend. The London branches of U.S. banks became their head office's single largest depositer as they transferred funds borrowed from the European banking systems. Thus, when money was tightened in the United States, the large international banks were able to borrow from their foreign branches to circumvent the Federal Reserve System's policy of monetary stringency.
London Gold Pool collapses; dollar loses its gold anchor

In April 1968 the United States withdrew from the London Gold Pool (to which it contributed half the gold sold), and the Pool's operations were promptly disbanded. The U.S. let it be known that further central-bank purchases of U.S. gold (with the surplus dollars being thrown onto the world economy by U.S. military spending in Southeast Asia and elsewhere) would be viewed as an "unfriendly act." Three years later, in August 1971, President Nixon closed the U.S. gold window officially and the dollar became inconvertible. Debt-money in the form of U.S. Treasury bills supplanted asset-money in the form of gold.
Benson-Fowler letters lock Canada into Treasury-bill standard

On December 16, 1968, Finance Minister Edgar Benson exchanged letters with the U.S. Treasury promising that Canada would keep all its international monetary reserves in the form of U.S. Treasury bills in exchange for continued Canadian access to U.S. capital markets. Indeed, Mr. Benson assured U.S. Treasury Secretary Henry Fowler, "the Canadian Government has invested its United States dollar reserves (in excess of working balances) in special non-marketable issues of the United States Treasury."
Nixon termina patrón oro: dólar libre

Three years later, in August 1971, President Nixon closed the U.S. gold window officially and the dollar became inconvertible. Debt-money in the form of U.S. Treasury bills supplanted asset-money in the form of gold. [...] Since 1971, gold has been supplanted by dollar credits, that is, by the U.S. Treasury securities held by central banks throughout the world, supplemented by Eurodollar deposits in — and borrowings from — the international banking system dominated by the large U.S. banks. This means that payment of interest on international borrowings can no longer be viewed as payment to foreign countries for "abstaining" from using their gold at home. It has become simply a payment for the ability by these countries and their banking systems to create credit by legal fiat and sheer risk-taking derring-do.
US food prices nearly quadruple, exposing price-inelasticity

Advocates of flexible exchange rates (mainly the Americans, whose falling dollar seemed to provide U.S. exporters with a competitive edge in world markets) claimed that exchange-rate variations would serve to stabilize international payments. [...] Many imports and exports are of a structural, price-inelastic nature and thus are not strongly influenced by shifting currency values. For instance, when U.S. food prices almost quadrupled in 1972/73, people did not eat less, they paid more. Similarly, when oil prices were subsequently quadrupled, people did not use less oil to heat their homes or power their cars; again they paid the higher prices.
Europe stops supporting the dollar; currencies float

In March 1973, in response to continued refusal by the United States to rectify its balance-of-payments deficit, European central banks stopped stabilizing the dollar's value. Prior to this time they had thrown their own currency onto foreign-exchange markets to purchase surplus dollars — and under the Treasury-bill standard they felt obliged to relend these dollars to the U.S. government. This process now came to an end. Without continued central-bank support the dollar fell in value, along with other currencies in payments-deficit status or tied to such currencies. The world of fixed exchange rates gave way to a period of flexible currency parities.
March 1973: foreign central banks stop absorbing surplus dollars

The plethora of domestic credit created during the Vietnam years encouraged large U.S. corporations to borrow for the purpose of buying out enterprises in foreign countries. But this situation ended when foreign central banks stopped accepting surplus dollars in March 1973. Canada can hardly emulate the U.S. experience in creating funds with which to take over foreign enterprises. However, the country may well increase its supply of domestic credit so as to induce Canadian corporations, provinces, and municipalities to borrow at home rather than abroad.
US blocks foreign equity above 5% in US firms

U.S. officials went so far as to suggest that foreign central banks invest their surplus dollars in the U.S. stock market. [...] Furthermore, dollars flowing into Canada and other countries in the process of U.S. investment takeovers of foreign firms would have been recycled to the U.S. stock and bond markets in the form of minority, non-decision-making positions. (The United States for its part announced its opposition to foreigners buying more than a 5 per cent equity in U.S. firms shortly after world oil prices quadrupled in 1973.)
Canada's trade balance peaks at $2.7 billion surplus

As events have worked out, the country's trade surplus has fallen rather than risen from its 1973 level of $2.7 billion. In 1974 it declined by $1 billion, and then fell by $2.2 billion more in 1975, showing a deficit for the first time in over fifteen years [...] Interest and dividend payments on foreign borrowings now represent the largest major single item in Canada's current-account deficit. The deficit on these payments nearly doubled between 1973 and 1976, when it reached $2.5 billion; in 1977, it hit $3.4 billion.
OPEC quadruples oil prices, structural payments deficits emerge

Since world energy prices quadrupled in 1973 in the wake of a world inflation in food and industrial prices, a number of nations have fallen into structural deficit in their international trade and payments. Unable to restrict their essential energy and food needs in response to higher world prices, and dependent on rather fixed annual quantities of replacement parts and other vital imports, they have not been able to increase their export quantities by enough to cover their higher import costs. As long as the world economy remains in recession, world raw-materials prices for commodities other than oil will remain far below their 1973 highs.
John Turner asks provinces to clear foreign borrowings — refused

However, given the realities of today's federal-provincial tensions, and in particular the sensitivities of the Quebec government, the federal government has faced severe constraints on its ability to implement economic policy. For instance; in April 1974, when Finance Minister John Turner asked Canadian provinces not to borrow abroad without clearance, his authority to make such a request was successfully challenged. The federal government could only induce provinces, municipalities, and corporations to curtail their foreign borrowing by providing them with a more attractive domestic market — and this presupposed a lower prospective rate of inflation.
FIRA established to screen foreign takeovers

More recently, the government has sought to spur indirect investment rather than direct foreign investment in Canada. In addition to establishing the Foreign Investment Review Agency (FIRA) to screen foreign direct takeovers, the government has refrained from levying the 15 per cent withholding tax on foreign income where the investor does not control a majority of the debtor company's common stock.
US Treasury debt exceeds gold; foreign banks finance the deficit

Foreign central banks hold another $20 billion in the form of U.S. bank deposits: these claims are some 91 per cent of the United States' total 1976 exports. They are enough to make countries somewhat reticent to let the U.S. dollar depreciate by as much as the nation's payments deficit would normally warrant. In fact, the world's central banks have continued to support the dollar (by buying surplus dollars with their own domestic currency), enabling the United States to run its foreign policy almost exclusively with a view toward domestic economic considerations.
Franklin National Bank fails; US banks turn abroad for earnings

With virtually unlimited sources of credit, the large U.S. banks showed themselves to be highly aggressive in lending to real estate investment trusts (REITs), oil-tanker companies, central banks in chronic payments-deficit countries, and other areas where they suffered large losses when the world economy turned down in 1974. A number of U.S. banks (led by Franklin National Bank in New York) became insolvent, while enormous losses were absorbed by international banks as a whole. Many banks sought to recoup their losses by moving aggressively into foreign markets, inspired by the success of Citibank of New York. Today, the great bulk of earnings by U.S. international banks comes from their foreign loans rather than from their domestic business.
Foreign investors own 53% of Canadian manufacturing

According to Statistics Canada figures, as of yearend 1975 foreign investors owned 53 per cent of Canadian manufacturing (with U.S. investors alone accounting for 44 per cent), 58 per cent of its mining and smelting, and 58 per cent of its petroleum and natural gas. Canada's ownership of its own resources is highest in the troubled textile industry and beverages (74 per cent), followed by the paper and pulp industry (72 per cent). The nation owns only 38 per cent of its agricultural machinery industry, 36 per cent of its electrical equipment industry, 32 per cent of its aluminum and petroleum industries, 30 per cent of its rubber industry, 27 per cent of its chemical industry, and 16 per cent of its automotive industry.
Canadian long-term foreign-currency debt doubles to $28 billion

As the world economy moved into recession in 1974, Canada's foreign borrowing increased sharply. The country's long-term foreign currency obligations doubled — from $14 billion at the beginning of 1974 to $28 billion by the end of 1976. Most of this amount was borrowed to finance public spending by the provinces and municipalities. Only a portion was to undertake new productive investments generating profits or foreign exchange to repay these debts.
Foreign earnings on Canadian investments hit $3.3 billion

In 1976 foreigners earned $3.3 billion on their investments in Canada, compared to the $0.8 billion earned by Canadians on their foreign investments. The resulting $2.5 billion deficit represents a sharp jump from the $1.9 billion in 1975, $1.6 billion in 1974, and the $1.3 billion in 1973. (During the 1960s the net deficit on interest and dividends has risen gradually upward to a $0.9 billion level in 1969.) Thus, Canada's growth in foreign borrowings has become the single major factor in the economy's deepening balance-of-payments deficit.
White paper limits foreign banks to 15% of commercial lending

In considering a legislative framework for foreign banks in Canada, [the white paper concludes], a basic conflict arises between the objectives of maximizing competition and ensuring that the control of our financial system remains predominantly in Canadian hands. [...] The (new Bank) Act will preclude the establishment in Canada of branches or agencies of foreign banks. Thus those foreign banks wishing to operate in Canada will be able to do so only through bank subsidiaries or non-bank affiliates which are Canadian persons subject only to Canadian laws. [...] The size of a foreign bank's subsidiary will be limited to 20 times its authorized capital. [...] Canadian regulatory policy, subject to review, will be to limit total operations of foreign banks to 15 per cent of total commercial lending in Canada.
US Steel lays off 15,000; capital consumption exceeds saving

A parallel development has been major layoffs, including 15 thousand employees in the steel industry in 1977. This unemployment results in massive income transfers from federal, state, and local governments in the form of unemployment insurance, welfare, social security, and the provision of make-work jobs, leading to even higher budget deficits at the federal level ($60 billion projected for 1977) as well as at state and local levels. These deficits will be occurring without a corresponding growth in the capital base to support a growing debt, whose projected interest and amortization threatens to "crowd out" private-sector borrowing in the absence of yet new credit pyramiding.
Foreign central banks fund 70% of US federal deficit growth

This policy has now evolved into "galloping benign neglect" as the U.S. trade deficit continues to grow. Of the $17 billion growth in the United States' publically held federal debt, and during January - July, 1977, foreign central banks used the proceeds of their trade surplus with the United States to buy $12 billion, that is, over 70 per cent.
Canada and Sweden forgive Third World aid loans

Today's payments-deficit countries have ceased to be good credit risks. They have borrowed up to the hilt, and world lenders are shying away from extending further loans, as is the case of Peru, Zaire, and several other countries. (Canada and Sweden have each recently forgiven over $200 million in foreign aid loans to Third World countries in recognition of the fact that these loans are virtually unrepayable in the face of the debtor countries' continued poverty.)
Canada's interest-and-dividend deficit hits $3.4 billion

Interest and dividend payments on foreign borrowings now represent the largest major single item in Canada's current-account deficit. The deficit on these payments nearly doubled between 1973 and 1976, when it reached $2.5 billion; in 1977, it hit $3.4 billion. (In addition, the repayment of principal, which appears on capital account, is now running at an annual rate of over $1 billion.) This scheduled debt service is not responsive to changes in currency values. Because it is denominated in U.S. dollars, and in even stronger European currencies such as the German mark, increasing sums of Canadian dollars are needed for debt service as Canada's domestic currency falls in value.
Arthur Burns denounces 'competition of laxity' in US bank regulation

Arthur Burns, former chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve System, recently drew attention to the "competition of laxity" of U.S. bank-regulatory authorities, and to a similar competition in loosening of loan standards by the banking system itself as private bankers have sought out new loan prospects almost irrespective of risk factors. Many U.S. banks have come to believe that the domestic and world economies are operating on a permanent government-bailout system in which insolvent borrowers — if they are large enough and important enough — will be lent ever-rising sums in order to maintain their solvency.
Canadian dollar allowed to float mid-1977

When Canada's currency was allowed to float in mid-1977, some observers hoped that depreciation would restore equilibrium to the country's international payments. Others pointed out that many Canadian exports were denominated in U.S. dollars, and that world demand for Canadian products was price-inelastic. This suggested that the nation would have to shift resources more into its export industries and import-displacing industries, and to promote its foreign trade in the face of mounting protectionism abroad.
Canada's debt service running above $3 billion per year

Meanwhile, Canada's foreign borrowing has left a legacy of required debt service for many years to come. Interest and dividend payments are now (mid-1978) running at an annual rate of over $3 billion, another $1 billion representing amortization of past loans. Meanwhile, trade policy on the part of Canada's customers — especially the United States — has become more protectionist, thereby limiting Canada's potential growth in exports. The result has been a sharp escalation in Canada's prospective payments deficit.
Canada now a satellite of the US Treasury-bill monetary system

Canada is prevented from pursuing these policies mainly because it is an economically small nation. If the Bank of Canada promotes easier credit, interest rates will fall and Canadian capital will flow to higher-interest countries. This will aggravate the payments deficit and put further downward pressure on the currency's international value. When Canada runs such deficits foreign central banks will not automatically relend this spending to the Bank of Canada by buying the country's federal debt. Canada cannot achieve the free ride enjoyed by the United States because there is no Canadian-dollar standard in international finance, only the U.S. Treasury-bill standard.
IMF austerity as instrument of creditor discipline

The tendency of wages to lag behind the general rate of inflation has long been observed to be of critical importance. It underlies the IMF's "austerity programs" designed to stabilize the balance-of-payments position of chronic payments-deficit countries. Even so, depreciation will lower the country's relative labour costs only to the extent that its workers do not react in a wave of strikes or political disturbances.
Canada risks becoming 'hewers of wood and drawers of water'

All of today's industrial nations have developed by means of protective tariffs whose revenues were used to fund a far-reaching system of internal improvements. [...] Countries that did not emulate the industrial nations, and which pursued their short-term advantage to the detriment of their long-term development, have fallen into the unenviable position of being hewers of wood and drawers of water. I have elaborated these views in my recent book Global Fracture: The New International Economic Order (Harper & Row: 1977).
